data.title: Shortest Mode
data.solution:
from re import Match, sub

def store_variable(match: Match[str]) -> str:
    var = match[0]
    if var[0] not in SEEN:
        SEEN.add(var[0])
        VARS[var] = var[0]
    return var


def convert_variable(match: Match[str]) -> str:
    var = match[0]
    if var in VARS:
        return VARS[var]

    # Try all same-case letters
    p = 65 if var[0].isupper() else 97
    for i in range(26):
        ch = chr(i + p)
        if ch in SEEN:
            continue
        SEEN.add(ch)
        VARS[var] = ch
        return ch
    
    # Try switching case
    ch = chr(ord(var[0]) ^ 32)
    if ch not in SEEN:
        SEEN.add(ch)
        VARS[var] = ch
        return ch
    
    # Try all switched-case letters
    for i in range(26):
        ch = chr(i + p ^ 32)
        if ch in SEEN:
            continue
        SEEN.add(ch)
        VARS[var] = ch
        return ch

    return var  # something went wrong


def convert_number(match: Match[str]) -> str:
    num = match[0]
    _num = num.rstrip("0")
    return min(num, f"{_num}e{len(num) - len(_num)}", key=len)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    VARS: dict[str, str] = {}
    SEEN: set[str] = set()

    s = ";".join(input() for _ in range(int(input())))
    # Reduce variable names
    s = sub(r"[a-zA-Z]+", store_variable, s)
    s = sub(r"[a-zA-Z]+", convert_variable, s)
    # Convert numbers
    s = sub(r"[0-9]+", convert_number, s)
    
    # Remove semicolons
    s = s.replace(" ", "").replace("\t", "").replace("*{;", "*{")
    res = ""
    stack: list[bool] = [False]
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch == "{":
            stack.append(i > 0 and s[i - 1] == "*")
        elif ch == "}":
            _ = stack.pop()
        elif ch == ";":
            if stack[-1] and i + 1 < len(s) and s[i + 1] == "}":
                continue
        res += ch
    
    print(res)
data.statement:
Congratulations, you've just coded a solution to a clash in <<CGL>> (a made-up coding language)! Unfortunately, you're playing the clash in Shortest Mode, which requires solutions to contain as few characters as possible.

To create the shortest possible code, you come up with a three-step plan:

1. <<Remove all whitespace characters>> from your code, except for newline (line break) characters, which you must <<replace with semi-colons>> ({{\n}} → {{;}}) for syntax correctness.

2. <<Reduce variable names to a single character>>. Variables in CGL consist only of English letters ({{A}}-{{Z}}, {{a}}-{{z}}) and do not contain other non-alphabetical characters (e.g., digits or underscores). You intend to <<use the first letter (with casing preserved)>> as the shortened variable name.

3. Convert numbers <<ending with some consecutive number of zeros>> into standard notation <<if the resulting notation is shorter>>. The standard notation of a number (e.g., {{1750000}}) is the non-zero starting portion of the number, followed by {{e}}, followed by the number of ending consecutive zeros (e.g., {{175e4}}).

This plan should work in theory, but alas, you hit the dreaded syntax error when testing! After some debugging, you find that the issues occur because of the following two reasons:

1. <<Incorrect semi-colon usage>>. It turns out that repeat blocks may not begin or end with semi-colons ({{;}}). You have to remove them yourself as and when they appear. A repeat block is marked by some variable/number, followed by the multiplication symbol ({{*}}), followed by the left curly brace ({{​{}}), followed by one or more lines of code, and ending with a right curly brace ({{}​}}). An example of a repeat block is as follows:
```Loop * {
someVar = Loop + 1
::​<​< someVar
Loop += Loop + someVar
}```2. <<De-duplicate variable names>>. You suspect there may be other variables with the same shortened name that got overridden. You then re-examine your code; on encountering the <<first duplicate shortened name>>, you intend to:
• Try to assign the <<first unused letter>> (from {{A}} to {{Z}}) as the new shortened variable name, while <<preserving casing>>
• If that fails, try to <<switch the case>> of the shortened variable name (e.g. {{s}} → {{S}})
• If that fails, try to assign the <<first unused letter>> (from {{A}} to {{Z}}) as the new shortened variable name, this time based on the <<switched casing>>. This is guaranteed to find a unique variable name.
This process is repeated until all variable names have been de-duplicated.

Hopefully your code will now be error-free and short enough to win! Good luck!

lastVersion.statementHTML:
Goal

Congratulations, you've just coded a solution to a clash in CGL (a made-up coding language)! Unfortunately, you're playing the clash in Shortest Mode, which requires solutions to contain as few characters as possible.

To create the shortest possible code, you come up with a three-step plan:

1. Remove all whitespace characters from your code, except for newline (line break) characters, which you must replace with semi-colons (\n → ;) for syntax correctness.

2. Reduce variable names to a single character. Variables in CGL consist only of English letters (A-Z, a-z) and do not contain other non-alphabetical characters (e.g., digits or underscores). You intend to use the first letter (with casing preserved) as the shortened variable name.

3. Convert numbers ending with some consecutive number of zeros into standard notation if the resulting notation is shorter. The standard notation of a number (e.g., 1750000) is the non-zero starting portion of the number, followed by e, followed by the number of ending consecutive zeros (e.g., 175e4).

This plan should work in theory, but alas, you hit the dreaded syntax error when testing! After some debugging, you find that the issues occur because of the following two reasons:

1. Incorrect semi-colon usage. It turns out that repeat blocks may not begin or end with semi-colons (;). You have to remove them yourself as and when they appear. A repeat block is marked by some variable/number, followed by the multiplication symbol (*), followed by the left curly brace (​{), followed by one or more lines of code, and ending with a right curly brace (}​). An example of a repeat block is as follows:
Loop * {
someVar = Loop + 1
::​<​< someVar
Loop += Loop + someVar
}
2. De-duplicate variable names. You suspect there may be other variables with the same shortened name that got overridden. You then re-examine your code; on encountering the first duplicate shortened name, you intend to:
• Try to assign the first unused letter (from A to Z) as the new shortened variable name, while preserving casing
• If that fails, try to switch the case of the shortened variable name (e.g. s → S)
• If that fails, try to assign the first unused letter (from A to Z) as the new shortened variable name, this time based on the switched casing. This is guaranteed to find a unique variable name.
This process is repeated until all variable names have been de-duplicated.

Hopefully your code will now be error-free and short enough to win! Good luck!




   

      
Input

      
Line 1: A positive integer numLines; the number of lines of CGL code.
Next numLines lines: The original CGL code.

   

   

      
Output

      
Line 1: The shortened CGL code.

   

   

      
Constraints

      
• 1 ≤ numLines ≤ 10
• 1 ≤ Input line length ≤ 50
• 1 ≤ Output length ≤ 100
• Whitespace characters used in the input will be limited to spaces, newlines (\n), and tabs (\t).
• Every occurrence of an English letter (A-Z, a-z) will always be part of some variable.
• The standard notation of a number will never have the same length as the original number.
• All numbers are valid 32-bit integers that do not contain leading zeros (except for 0 itself). Numbers given in the input will not be expressed in standard notation.
• The given CGL code will not contain any semi-colons (;).

   

   

      
Example

      

         

            
Input

            
3
first = 1
second = 2
(first == second) ? first : second

         

         

            
Output

            
f=1;s=2;(f==s)?f:s
